claims.text: A dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure imparts creep resistance to the protective coating.
A high density of incoherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries obstructs dislocation motion.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries delay recovery processes.
The FCC regions accommodate plastic strain through twinning and limited slip.
The BCC phase deforms mainly by slip.
Strain is partitioned between the FCC and BCC/B2 phases.
Interphase-boundary barriers and FCC/BCC strain partitioning delay steady-state creep.
The starting coating contains both FCC and BCC or B2 phases.
The starting coating consists of 〈001〉-oriented FCC dendrites interpenetrated by a network of BCC/B2 precipitates or interdendritic regions.
Changing deposition parameters can systematically alter dendrite size, precipitate distribution, and FCC/BCC interphase-boundary density.
The BCC phase is less twinnable than the FCC phase.
FCC/BCC interfaces cause dislocation pile-ups and thereby increase work hardening.
Differential FCC twinning and BCC slip generate internal stress fields at FCC/BCC boundaries.
Boundary-associated internal stress fields further impede dislocation motion and delay the onset of diffusion-assisted creep.
At identical stress and temperature, coatings with higher FCC/BCC boundary density will have lower creep strain rates than coarser coatings.
At identical stress and temperature, coatings with higher FCC/BCC boundary density will have longer creep-rupture lives than coarser coatings.
The processed high-boundary-density coating will show less steady-state creep deformation than the as-deposited baseline.
The proposed boundary-controlled mechanism dominates when dislocation-mediated deformation is active but diffusion creep is not dominant.
The operating temperature must remain below the regime of full recrystallization or phase transformation.
The apparent influence of interphase-boundary density may depend on composition and local stress state.
